analysis.one_liner: Caps malpractice payouts, cuts lawyers' fees, and steers injury disputes out of court.
analysis.headline: The bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee in October 1991 and died there without a hearing, markup, or vote before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The American Health Quality Act would have rewritten malpractice law nationwide: capping compensation for pain and suffering at $250,000, capping lawyers' fees at 15-25% of awards, barring punitive damages against drug and device makers whose products were FDA-approved, and shortening the time patients have to sue. It would have paid states bonus Medicaid funds to move malpractice disputes into arbitration-style systems instead of court, funded programs to prevent medical injuries, and created a group-purchasing insurance plan to cut liability costs for community health centers. It never advanced past committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Doctors, hospitals, malpractice insurers, and drug and device manufacturers would have gained the most, since the bill's core titles cap damages, limit lawyers' fees, shorten filing deadlines, and shield FDA-approved products from punitive damages. Community and migrant health centers would have gained a federally funded insurance pool to lower their liability premiums. States adopting the bill's arbitration and injury-prevention programs would have received small bonus Medicaid payments.

how_it_helps.text: Caps on non-economic damages ($250,000), attorney fees (25% of the first $150,000, 15% above that), and punitive damages were aimed at lowering malpractice insurance premiums and health care costs, which Congress found were driven up by litigation and defensive medicine [S2] [S3].

States would have received enhanced Medicaid bonus payments to build alternative dispute resolution systems resolving malpractice claims outside court, with federal grants for private-sector demonstration programs [S2] [S3].
A federally funded risk retention group would have let community and migrant health centers band together to buy professional liability insurance, reducing their costs [S2] [S3].
Bonus payments would also reward states that strengthened medical disciplinary boards, added public members, and ran injury-prevention programs [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Patients injured by malpractice would have borne the cost: their compensation for pain, suffering, disfigurement, and lost enjoyment of life would have been capped at $250,000 no matter how severe the injury or how many providers were at fault, their lawyers' fees capped, their filing window shortened to two years from discovery and four years from the injury, and federal law would have overridden any state that offered stronger protections. Drug and device makers would have been shielded from punitive damages whenever their product had FDA approval.

drawbacks.text: The $250,000 cap on non-economic damages would fall hardest on catastrophically injured patients — children, retirees, and people without lost wages — whose economic damages are small but whose suffering is greatest [S3].

Capping contingency fees at 15-25% could make it harder for injured patients to find a lawyer willing to take a costly, uncertain malpractice case, effectively narrowing access to the courthouse [S3].
The bill would have preempted state laws, overriding any state's longer filing periods, higher damage limits, or stronger patient protections [S3].

A two-year deadline from when an injury 'should reasonably have been discovered,' with an absolute four-year cutoff, could bar claims for harms that surface slowly, such as birth injuries or delayed cancer diagnoses [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill packaged genuinely useful ideas — injury prevention, stronger state medical boards, cheaper liability insurance for community health centers, and faster dispute resolution — with a hard-favored shift of risk away from providers and manufacturers. Its centerpiece provisions (damage caps, fee caps, shorter deadlines, an FDA-approval shield against punitive damages, and federal preemption of stronger state laws) reduce accountability for negligent care, and the patient-safety benefits come with the caps rather than because of them. Weighing it honestly, the parts helping health centers and state quality programs are real but secondary; the main effect would have been to cut what injured patients can recover.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on October 17, 1991, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and sat there with no hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Sen. Dave Durenberger introduced the bill in the Senate on October 17, 1991, joined by Sens. Danforth and Burns [S1] [S3] [S5].
Four Senate Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did [S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the day it was introduced, and no further action appears in the record for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The bill's tort-reform provisions arrived amid the early-1990s debate over health care costs, but Congress enacted no such national malpractice overhaul in the 102nd Congress [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Injured patients kept the full malpractice remedies their states provide — uncapped damages, ordinary lawyer fees, and no FDA shield for drug and device makers. Community health centers did not get the subsidized insurance pool the bill offered, so its possible benefits to them were also lost.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured patients and the plaintiffs' bar

for.name: Sen. Dave Durenberger
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

for.name: Sens. John Danforth and Conrad Burns
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as its original cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and never scheduled a hearing or markup, letting it expire at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and all four cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the bill died in committee without a vote, so no roll calls reveal any cross-party support.

industries.note: Damage caps, fee caps, shorter filing deadlines, and a higher proof standard in delivery-room cases would have cut malpractice exposure and premiums. The cost falls on patients with the worst injuries, though providers argued lower premiums ease access to high-risk care like obstetrics.

Caps on non-economic damages, mandatory periodic payments, collateral-source offsets, and the shortened filing window all shrink the payouts insurers must make; their savings come directly out of what injured patients can collect.

The bill bars punitive damages against any drug or device maker whose product was FDA-approved, unless the company withheld or misrepresented information to the FDA — a major shield from liability for product-related harm.
A federally capitalized risk retention group would have let these safety-net clinics pool and buy professional liability insurance at lower cost, freeing money for care.

Fee caps of 15-25% and the arbitration push would have cut lawyers' contingency recoveries, and because lawyers decline cases they cannot afford, that also narrows patients' practical access to counsel.
